buildings.name: Casa Romuli (Hut of Romulus)
buildings.summary: A wattle-and-daub hut with a thatched roof on the Germalus, kept up and rebuilt in the same form as the house of Romulus; burned in 38 and 12 BC and renewed each time, still listed in the 4th-century Regionary catalogue. Postholes of three Iron Age huts of the 8th century BC were found beside the Scalae Caci.

phases.t: burned during a sacrifice and rebuilt

scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 74

buildings.name: Lupercal
buildings.summary: The cave at the foot of the SW Palatine where the she-wolf suckled the twins, with a spring and a sacred fig, starting point of the Lupercalia run; a bronze wolf with the twins was set up here by the Ogulnii in 296 BC.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 238
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) III s.v. Lupercal (Coarelli)
buildings.note: Exact site unknown; the vaulted nymphaeum found in 2007 below the House of Augustus is disputed.

buildings.name: Lupercal (Augustan)
buildings.summary: Restored by Augustus as part of his Palatine programme. The Lupercalia were celebrated until Pope Gelasius suppressed them in 494.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 238

buildings.name: Temple of Victoria
buildings.summary: Built by L. Postumius Megellus from fines collected as aedile and dedicated on 1 August 294 BC as consul: the first hexastyle temple with lateral colonnades since the Capitoline temple, perhaps the first with stone columns and a closed sculpted pediment, on a podium 33 x 19 m at the brow of the hill above the Lupercal, the Palatine counterpart of Jupiter on the Capitol. The black stone of the Magna Mater was kept in it from 204 to 191 BC.

phases.t: sacred stone of Magna Mater housed here

scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 420

buildings.name: Temple of Victoria (late Republican restoration)
buildings.summary: Restored in the third quarter of the 1st century BC with travertine Corinthian columns and an internal colonnade in the cella, on the old plan.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 420
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) V s.v. Victoria, aedes (Pensabene)

buildings.name: Shrine of Victoria Virgo
buildings.summary: Shrine dedicated by Cato the Elder in 193 BC next to the temple of Victory; Coarelli identified it with the small building long called the Auguratorium, aligned with the Magna Mater.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 421
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) V s.v. Victoria Virgo (Coarelli)

buildings.name: Temple of Magna Mater
buildings.summary: Begun in 204 BC for the black stone of the Phrygian Mother brought from Pessinus at the Sibyl's bidding to drive Hannibal from Italy, and dedicated by M. Iunius Brutus on 10 April 191; its broad stair served as seating for the plays of the Megalesia performed on the platform below.

buildings.name: Temple of Magna Mater (rebuilt after 111 BC)
buildings.summary: Burned in 111 BC and rebuilt on a higher concrete podium, with a basin for ritual ablutions at the foot of the stair.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 242-243

buildings.name: Temple of Magna Mater (Augustan)
buildings.summary: Burned again in AD 3 and rebuilt by Augustus as a hexastyle Corinthian prostyle temple, shown on the Villa Medici relief with the goddess' throne in the pediment; the cult lasted to the end of paganism.

buildings.name: House of Livia
buildings.summary: A late Republican house of about 75-50 BC entered down a sloping corridor, with an atrium and painted rooms in the Second Style; part of Augustus' residence and identified with Livia from a lead pipe naming Iulia Augusta. Later preserved beneath the raised levels of the imperial palace.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 130
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

buildings.name: House of Augustus (first house)
buildings.summary: Octavian bought the house of the orator Hortensius and neighbouring properties on the Palatine; Carettoni's excavations uncovered rooms of this first house with Second Style paintings, partly filled in when the Apollo terrace was built.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 123
Carettoni, Das Haus des Augustus auf dem Palatin (1983)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

buildings.name: House of Augustus
buildings.summary: After lightning struck part of the property in 36 BC Augustus dedicated it to Apollo and rebuilt his house beside the temple, modest in decoration (the 'Room of the Masks', the 'studiolo'), with laurels and the civic crown over its door from 27 BC; part was made public when he became pontifex maximus in 12 BC.

phases.t: laurels and corona civica on the doorposts
a shrine of Vesta set up in the house

scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 123

buildings.name: Shrine of Vesta on the Palatine
buildings.summary: When Augustus became pontifex maximus on 6 March 12 BC he set up a shrine of Vesta in his house so that he need not live in the Domus Publica.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 413
buildings.note: Site in the House of Augustus unknown.

buildings.name: House of the Griffins
buildings.summary: A house of about 100 BC with some of the earliest Second Style paintings and a stucco lunette of two griffins, buried under the Domus Flavia.

buildings.name: Aula Isiaca
buildings.summary: An apsed hall of the 20s BC painted with Egyptian cult symbols, buried by the basilica of Domitian's palace; the paintings are now in the Loggia Mattei.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

buildings.name: Curiae Veteres
buildings.summary: The old meeting places of the thirty curiae at the NE corner of the Palatine, where the curiate priests held their common meals; archaic votive deposits (temenoi) have been found here under the Vigna Barberini slope.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 104
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) I s.v. Curiae Veteres (Panella)

buildings.name: Curiae Veteres (Augustan-Claudian)
buildings.summary: Rebuilt in the early Empire; swept away by Nero's works after 64.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 104

buildings.name: Temple of Apollo Palatinus
buildings.summary: Vowed after Naulochus, built on land of Augustus' house struck by lightning and dedicated on 9 October 28 BC as the thank-offering for Actium: solid Luna marble on a high podium, hexastyle with a gilded chariot of the Sun on the roof, ivory doors carved with the Niobids and the Gauls at Delphi, and statues by Scopas, Cephisodotus and Timotheus. The Sibylline Books were kept under the cult statue. It burned on the night of 18-19 March 363.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 14

buildings.name: Portico of the Danaids
buildings.summary: Colonnades of giallo antico around the temple precinct with statues of the fifty daughters of Danaus between the columns and their husbands as equestrian figures in front; Myron's four bronze cattle stood round the altar.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 14

buildings.name: Libraries of Apollo (Latin and Greek)
buildings.summary: Twin apsed halls for Latin and Greek books beside the temple, where the Senate also met in Augustus' old age; restored after 64 and again by Domitian, they appear on the Marble Plan.

buildings.name: Domus Tiberiana (Tiberian palace)
buildings.summary: The first imperial palace proper, built for Tiberius on the NW Palatine over late Republican houses; Tacitus calls it the 'domus Tiberiana'. Recent excavation shows that little of the visible platform belongs to him.

buildings.name: Domus Tiberiana with Caligula's extension to the Forum
buildings.summary: Caligula extended the palace down to the Forum, making the Temple of Castor its vestibule so that he could stand between the twin gods to be worshipped, and was murdered in a passage of the palace in January 41.

phases.t: Caligula killed in a cryptoporticus of the palace

buildings.name: Domus Tiberiana (Neronian platform)
buildings.summary: After the fire of 64 the palace was rebuilt on a vast vaulted platform about 150 x 120 m with a central peristyle and an encircling cryptoporticus, the structure under the later Farnese gardens; Galba was killed in 69 after leaving from here.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 136-137

buildings.name: Domus Tiberiana (Domitianic)
buildings.summary: Domitian added the multi-storey arcaded substructures along the Nova Via and linked the palace to his Forum vestibule by the covered ramp.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 136-137

buildings.name: Domus Tiberiana (Hadrianic)
buildings.summary: Hadrian extended the arcades on the Forum side toward the Clivus Victoriae; Antoninus Pius lived here before his accession. In the 7th century the Forum-side halls served Byzantine officials and later the popes.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 136-137

buildings.name: Domus Transitoria
buildings.summary: Nero's first palace, linking the Palatine to the gardens of Maecenas on the Esquiline; under the Domus Flavia survive a sunken court with a nymphaeum of cascading water and marble-inlaid pavilions with painted vaults. Destroyed in the fire of 64.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 138
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) II s.v. Domus Transitoria (De Vos)

buildings.name: Rotating dining hall of the Domus Aurea (Vigna Barberini)
buildings.summary: A tower-like round structure with a central pillar 4 m thick found in 2009 at the NE corner of the Vigna Barberini, identified with the main dining room of the Golden House that 'turned day and night like the heavens'. Buried under the Flavian terrace.
scholarship: Villedieu, in Neronia Electronica 1 (2011)
